blocks.text: [III, 21] σὶς [sis]: Catarractes, a species of sea bird. Eustathius on Dionysius: Τὶ ὄρνεον ἀετῶδες καταῤῥάκτης καλεῖται [ti orneon aetōdes katarrhaktēs kaleitai]: A certain bird of the eagle kind is called catarrhactes. Aristophanes in the Birds: Καὶ ἐρωδιῷ, καὶ καταῤῥάκτῃ, καὶ μελαγκορύφῳ [kai erōdiō, kai katarrhaktē, kai melankoryphō]: And to the heron, and to the catarrhactes, and to the blackcap. And there the Scholiast: Καταῤῥάκται εἰσὶ παρὰ Καλλιμάχῳ ἀναγεγραμμέναι [Katarrhaktai eisi para Kallimachō anagegrammenai]: Catarractae are described by Callimachus. Aristotle, History, book 2, chapter 17: Νῆττα δὲ, καὶ χὴν, καὶ λάρος, καὶ καταῤῥάκτης, καὶ ὠτὶς τὸν στόμαχον εὐρὺν καὶ πλατὺν ὅλον ἔχουσι [Nētta de, kai chēn, kai laros, kai katarrhaktēs, kai ōtis ton stomachon euryn kai platyn holon echousi]: The duck, the goose, the gull, the catarrhactes and the bustard have the whole stomach wide and broad. And book 9, chapter 12: Ὁ δὲ καταῤῥάκτης ζῇ μὲν περὶ θάλατταν. ὅταν δὲ καθῇ ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ βαθὺ, μένει χρόνον οὐκ ἐλάττονα, ἢ ὅσον πλέθρον διέλθοι τις. ἔστι δ᾽ ἔλαττον ἱέρακος τὸ ὄρνεον [Ho de katarrhaktēs zē men peri thalattan. hotan de kathē heauton eis to bathy, menei chronon ouk elattona, ē hoson plethron dielthoi tis. esti d' elatton hierakos to orneon]: The catarrhactes lives by the sea. When it has plunged into the deep, it stays there no less time than it takes a man to walk across a plethrum. The bird is smaller than a hawk. Oppian in the Ixeutica writes that it is προσόμοιον [prosomoion], similar, to the goshawk. In Eustathius it is said to be called catarrhactes ὡς ἄνωθεν καταῤῥάσσων ἐν τῷ θηρεύειν τὰ ὄρνεα [hōs anōthen katarrhassōn en tō thēreuein ta ornea], as rushing down from above when it hunts birds. Wrongly, since the catarrhactes hunts nothing but fish. It is better, therefore, to learn the reason for the name from elsewhere. And Gesner's Excerpts from Oppian's Ixeutica, which indeed no longer survive, offer themselves conveniently. He had read a manuscript Greek paraphrase of them, in which the following is most to the point [book II, ch. 2]. 1. The catarractes sits on crags, shores and rocks that stand out above the water, which they call χοιράδας [choiradas], etc. And when it has seen some fish swimming (for it is very sharp-sighted, even down to the bottom of the sea), it flies higher, and with all its feathers drawn in, as if falling into the sea, it is borne through the intervening space of air faster than any dart, and plunges to the depth of an ell, until it has seized a fish and drawn it out; then, flying up, it devours it while it is still struggling ^{(3)}. Our most learned Vossius, in that excellent work of his on Mela, page β, quotes this in Greek from his manuscripts thus: Πρὸς ὕψος ἑαυτὸν αἴρει, καὶ τὰ πτερὰ πάντα συστείλας, εἰς τὸν πόντον, [col. 279] οἷα πίπτων, οἴσεται, διατεμὼν τὸν ἀέρα, παντὸς ἂν εἴποις βέλους ὀξύτερον, καὶ καταδύεται μέχρι ὀργυιᾶς, ἢ καὶ πλέον, ἔσθ᾽ ὅτε συλλαβὼν τὸν ἰχθὺν ἀνασπᾷ, καὶ ἀνιπτάμενος ἔτι πάλλοντα κατεσθίει [Pros hypsos heauton airei, kai ta ptera panta systeilas, eis ton ponton, hoia piptōn, oisetai, diatemōn ton aera, pantos an eipois belous oxyteron, kai katadyetai mechri orgyias, ē kai pleon, esth' hote syllabōn ton ichthyn anaspa, kai aniptamenos eti pallonta katesthiei]. 2. The death of the catarrhactes is harder than that which befalls any of the birds of uncertain life. For the keenness of their eyes, dulled when they are worn out by age, causes them, thinking they are hurling themselves headlong into the sea after fish as prey, to dash against crags and cliffs and perish [III, 22] ^{(4)}. 3. Catarrhactae are caught with images of fish painted on boards. For while they rush at these as if at live fish, they dash against them and perish ^{(5)}. 4. The male carries the eggs from which he guesses a male will be produced, the female those from which a female will come, up into the air, grasped in their talons. Then they drop them into the sea, and repeat this again and again for some days. The eggs being warmed by this motion, the chicks are hatched. 5. The chicks of the catarrhacta, as soon as they have seen the light, make no delay in the nest but strive to follow their parents in flight. Taken up by the parents, they are let down into the sea and at once drawn out again, so that with the help of their parents this kind of exercise may become easier for them. You see, reader, how fittingly it is called שלך in Hebrew and καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs] in Greek. For at one point it is described as משליך נפשו, ἑαυτὸν καταῤῥάσσων [heauton katarrhassōn], casting itself down, either deliberately into the sea, from which its food is supplied, or by mistake onto crags or painted boards, whence certain destruction for it; at another as משליך ביציו או בניו, throwing its eggs or letting its chicks down into the sea. To this last, perhaps, τὸ καταῤῥάσσειν [to katarrhassein] does not so properly apply, since it is not done with violence; but the Hebrew השליך means both to let down gently and to throw with violence. It is used of throwing headlong in Ion. II, 4., where the Prophet, using this verb, complains that he had been cast into the deep, into the heart of the sea. And in 2 Par. XXV, 12., where we read of ten thousand Edomites: וישליכום, And they threw them from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces. Accordingly the Greeks render: Καὶ κατεκρήμνιζον αὐτούς [Kai katekrēmnizon autous]; and Jerome: And they cast them headlong. But it is taken for letting down when it is written of Jeremiah in Ierem. XXXVIII, 6.: וישליכו אותו אל הבור, And they cast him into the pit, that is, they let him down. For it follows by way of explanation that he was let down there with ropes. So the catarrhactes, although it does not so much throw as let down its chicks into the sea, and perhaps its eggs too, could nevertheless be called שלך for that reason as well. And I would suppose the Hebrews had caught some scent of this account when they relate, on the authority of Aben Ezra, that the שלך is a bird that is accustomed להשליך ילדיו, to throw out its young. So much for the Greek version; since it is true, it is fitting to weigh the others against it as well.
